strengths: The paper proposes a clean and well-motivated conceptual framework: it distinguishes 'strong evaluability' (arbitrary-precision ranking from finite samples) from 'c-weak evaluability' (ranking up to multiplicative/additive error), and separates this from the classical notion of estimability. This formalization of 'when can generative models be reliably ranked from held-out data' is a useful lens for a practically important question.

Theorem 3.2 gives a crisp dichotomy for binary-valued IPMs (strong evaluability iff finite VC dimension; otherwise 3-weak evaluability, with the factor 3 shown tight by importing the lower bound of Bousquet et al. 2019). The proof is short but correct in structure, leveraging existing density-estimation machinery appropriately.

Theorem 3.6 (no finite taxonomy of sample complexities for estimable IPMs) is an original and interesting negative result, established via an explicit diagonalizing construction over scaled Boolean test classes; it shows that no VC-dimension-like single parameter governs sample complexity of estimable metrics.

The negative results on Rényi/KL divergences and the coverage profile are simple but illuminating: constructions of models that are indistinguishable under finite sampling yet differ sharply in metric value, formalizing the 'rare event' pathology of perplexity-based evaluation. The connection to the empirical literature questioning perplexity (Fang et al. 2025; Hu et al. 2024; Pillutla et al. 2021) gives the work practical relevance.

The analysis of perplexity as a score function (Theorem 5.3 and Proposition 5.5) is a nice contribution: it characterizes when nll/perplexity can and cannot evaluate TV distance, identifying a geometric-misalignment principle ('metrics that tolerate rare errors cannot be evaluated by scores that amplify them'). The Hellinger/Markov argument in the proof of Proposition 5.5 is elegant.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper clearly states which dichotomies are incomplete (the real-valued IPM case lacks the c'<3 lower bound), explicitly poses open questions, and discusses why margin/ratio assumptions are needed. No ethics concerns arise for a purely theoretical work.
weaknesses: Several central results are close relatives of prior work rather than fundamentally new machinery. The upper and lower bounds for the unbounded-VC-dimension regime of Theorem 3.2 are essentially imported from Bousquet et al. (2019), and the proof of Proposition 3.4's second bullet explicitly reuses that argument; the genuinely new content in these places is mainly the reframing under the evaluability definition.

The characterization is incomplete in the real-valued case: Proposition 3.4 establishes only one-sided results (strong evaluability under finite fat-shattering dimension; 3-weak evaluability under unbounded dimension) without a matching lower bound, so the advertised 'nearly complete characterization of IPM evaluability' overstates the binary case's completeness relative to the real-valued case, which arguably matters more for practice (e.g., Wasserstein-type metrics).

Some conclusions are fairly predictable. That unbounded losses (Theorem 3.8) and Rényi/KL divergences (Theorem 4.2) are not evaluable from finite samples follows from well-understood concentration failures; the value lies in the formalization more than in surprise. This limits the significance of the negative results individually.

The positive results carry strong and practically restrictive assumptions: Proposition 5.5 requires one candidate model to be Δ-close in ratio with Δ ≤ O(ε²), which is a very strong semi-realizability condition; Theorem 4.8 requires both a coverage lower bound on q* and a margin condition on the likelihood ratio. The paper acknowledges this, but the practical applicability of the positive results is limited.

Minor technical and presentational issues: the definition of the 'taxonomy' (Definition 3.5) permits a countable list while the theorem and surrounding discussion speak of a 'finite taxonomy,' creating a slight mismatch; Theorem 3.8's proof defines 'the distribution q̂ = (1/m) Σ g(x_i)' which is a number, not a distribution; page 13 references 'Assumption 5.4' where Assumption 4.7 is meant; several proofs rely on informal steps (e.g., 'any score function will rank the models incorrectly') that would benefit from more careful adversary arguments.

The framework assumes exact density access to models q (score functions take model identity q as input), and i.i.d. evaluation data; there is no discussion of how this maps onto realistic generative-model evaluation where models are accessed via samples or APIs, and no experiments or even illustrative simulations connect the theory to practice. For an ICML submission, some grounding of the abstract framework in realistic evaluation scenarios would strengthen significance.

Reproducibility is conceptual rather than empirical: all results are theorems with proofs in the appendix, which is fine for a theory paper, but there is no code, and some sample-complexity claims hide constants in ways that a reader cannot verify without completing omitted steps.

strengths: The paper asks a well-motivated and clean question: which evaluation metrics for generative models can be reliably computed/compared from finite held-out samples, and it formalizes this via a two-tier notion of evaluability (strong vs. weak) that is a reasonable abstraction of how empirical scores are used to rank models.

The negative results are conceptually crisp: the constructions showing that α-Rényi and KL divergences (and the coverage profile of Chen et al., 2025) are not weakly evaluable, because their values can hinge on rare events invisible in finite samples, are simple, correct, and give a principled explanation for known empirical pathologies of perplexity.

Theorem 3.6 (no finite taxonomy of sample complexities for estimable IPMs) is a genuinely interesting structural contribution, showing that unlike supervised learning there is no VC-like universal complexity parameter for estimating evaluation metrics.

The analysis of perplexity (Theorem 5.3, Proposition 5.5) that isolates when the nll score can/cannot evaluate TV distance, via a Hellinger-distance/Markov argument, is a nice touch connecting the abstract framework to the most practically used score.
Honest open-questions section: the paper clearly delineates what is proved (binary IPM dichotomy) from what is not (optimality of factor 3 for real-valued IPMs, evaluability of β-restricted KL).
weaknesses: Apparent soundness issue in Theorem 4.8: the proposed score function s(q, Seval) = Σ_{x∈supp(q⋆)} q̂(x)·1[q̂(x)/q(x) ≥ N] depends on the ground-truth distribution q⋆ (through supp(q⋆)), which violates Definition 2.2/2.3, where the score function must be a fixed map M × X* → R independent of q⋆. Since Assumption 4.6 only lower-bounds mass on the support without making it known, the positive result as stated does not fit the framework's own rules.

The lower-bound half of the 'dichotomy' in Theorem 3.2 (no c′ < 3 weak evaluability) is dispatched in one sentence via a reduction to Theorem 19 of Bousquet et al. (2019). The reduction from c′-weak evaluability of an IPM score function to a proper density-estimation algorithm with factor c′ is nontrivial (the score function need not output a distribution) and is not proved; for a headline 'strict dichotomy' claim, this needs a rigorous argument.

The positive results are largely direct applications of classical uniform-convergence machinery (VC/fat-shattering bounds, Yatracos-style estimators from Bousquet et al. 2019) to IPMs; the genuinely new technical content is mostly a collection of small adversarial constructions on 2–3 point domains, which limits the depth of the contribution.

Several proofs contain sloppiness that undermines confidence: in Theorem 3.8 q̂ is called a 'distribution' but is a mean of g(x_i); Hoeffding is applied while the boundedness assumption is stated only as g(x) ≤ B rather than |g(x)| ≤ B; Definition 2.4 has a typo ('ground-truth model g⋆'); the discussion after Theorem 4.8 cites a nonexistent 'Assumption 5.4' (should be 4.7); various rendering artifacts (broken O(·) expressions, 'Oe', garbled citations) appear throughout.

The weak evaluability definition (Definition 2.3) permits the sample size function and score function to depend on the candidate pair {q1, q2}, which is a permissive modeling choice; the paper does not discuss how results would change under a score function that must handle a pool of many candidate models, even though this is the practical scenario the introduction motivates.

Positioning relative to prior work is thin: non-estimability of divergences and TV over large domains, minimax lower bounds for f-divergence estimation, and the hypothesis-testing/competitive-ratio literature are not discussed, so it is hard to gauge how much of the negative-result landscape is genuinely new versus folklore.

The practical payoff is limited: the positive results require strong conditions (finite VC/fat-shattering dimension of the test class, or margin/closeness assumptions), and the negative results rely on adversarial near-degenerate pairs; the paper offers little guidance on which regime realistic generative-model evaluation falls into, and the framework's implications for benchmark or human-feedback evaluation (the alternatives it motivates against) are unexplored.

strengths: The paper introduces a clean and well-motivated formal framework ('evaluability') that captures, in a unified way, when a generative-model evaluation metric can be reliably ranked from finite held-out samples. The distinction between strong evaluability, weak evaluability, and estimability is crisp and the framework is general enough to cover both test-based metrics and likelihood-ratio-based divergences.

The evaluability characterization for IPMs is a genuinely useful contribution: the strict dichotomy for binary test classes (strongly evaluable iff finite VC dimension, otherwise exactly 3-weakly evaluable, with a matching lower bound via Bousquet et al. 2019) is a satisfying and complete result, and the extension to real-valued classes via fat-shattering dimension is a natural and mostly correct generalization.

The negative results for alpha-Renyi and KL divergence (Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3) use simple, transparent two-point constructions that cleanly isolate the 'rare event' pathology, and the coverage-profile analysis (discontinuity at the threshold N, margin assumption in Theorem 4.8) gives real insight into why naive truncation fixes fail.

The perplexity/NLL analysis (Section 5) connects the abstract framework to a practically important debate: showing that NLL cannot weakly evaluate TV or beta-restricted KL without ratio-closeness assumptions, while recovering a positive result under a semi-realizability condition, gives practitioners a principled account of when perplexity-based ranking is meaningful.

Proofs are provided in full in the appendix, the writing is generally clear, and the paper is honest about open problems (e.g., optimality of the factor 3 for real-valued IPMs, estimability vs. strong evaluability), which is appropriate for a framework-building paper.
weaknesses: A substantial portion of the positive machinery is a re-derivation or direct extension of known learning-theory results: the finite-VC case follows from standard uniform convergence plus Sauer's lemma, and the 3-weak evaluability and factor-3 optimality are imported from Yatracos (1985) and Bousquet et al. (2019). The impossibility constructions, while elegant, are fairly expected for unbounded metrics. The novelty rests mainly on the framing rather than on technically deep new tools.

There is a proof gap in Theorem 3.2's lower bound: the claim that a c'-weakly evaluable IPM with c' < 3 'implies that we can properly do density estimation with multiplicative factor c' < 3, which conflicts with Theorem 19 in Bousquet et al. (2019)' is asserted without a reduction. Weak evaluability only guarantees correct pairwise ranking up to a multiplicative factor, which is not transitive; extracting a proper selection algorithm with factor c' < 3 from pairwise comparisons requires an argument (e.g., about tournaments or two-candidate instances) that is not given, and the cited lower bound applies to proper algorithms. This central optimality claim needs a rigorous reduction.

The quantifier structure of Definition 2.3 is ambiguous and load-bearing: the sample-size function m_evl may not depend on (q1, q2), but the score function s apparently may. This should be stated explicitly, since several constructions (and the strength of the negative results) hinge on what information s may use; similarly, the taxonomy definition (Definition 3.5) permits the 'sufficiently small' threshold to depend on (q1, q2), which weakens Theorem 3.6 and deserves discussion.

The framework assumes models are given as explicit distributions (score functions evaluate q on arbitrary points, and q-hat-based scores require density evaluation). This limits practical reach for modern generative models (e.g., samplers without likelihood access), and the paper does not discuss this scope limitation; there is also no limitations section, which ICML expects.

Several results are weaker than their binary counterparts without full explanation of whether the gap is inherent: Proposition 3.4's second bullet does not establish optimality of the factor 3 (acknowledged), and Theorem 4.8's guarantee holds only under both a margin and a lower-bound assumption, so the 'additional conditions' in Table 1 are quite strong.

Presentation defects: cross-reference errors (e.g., 'Assumption 5.4' cited where Assumption 4.7 is meant on pages 10 and 13), a garbled author name in the Pillutla et al. (2021) reference, minor typos in Definition 2.4 ('g*' instead of 'q*', '{x1,...,xm)}'), and malformed Table 1 entries. While individually minor, in a theory paper precise statements and cross-references matter.

The practical guidance extracted from the theory remains fairly abstract ('score functions need to be aligned with geometric properties of metrics'); the paper does not translate its evaluability dichotomies into concrete recommendations (e.g., which bounded test classes to use in practice) or illustrate the phenomena empirically, even at a toy level.

strengths: The paper poses a well-motivated and cleanly formalized question: which evaluation metrics for generative models can be reliably computed or used for model ranking from finite IID samples? The two-tier definition of evaluability (strong vs. c-weak) in Definitions 2.3–2.4 is natural, and the summary table (Table 1) gives a clear map of the results.

The IPM analysis is the strongest part. The dichotomy in Theorem 3.2 (finite VC dimension ⟹ estimable/strongly evaluable; infinite VC ⟹ only 3-weak evaluable) meaningfully extends the TV-distance results of Bousquet et al. (2019) to general binary test classes, and Proposition 3.4 gives the real-valued analogue via fat-shattering dimension. The upper-bound arguments (uniform convergence, Yatracos-style scores) are clean.

Theorem 3.6 (no finite taxonomy of sample complexities for estimable IPMs) is a genuinely novel and interesting result: it shows there is no VC-like single parameter governing the sample complexity of estimable IPMs. The diagonal construction over scaled Boolean classes on disjoint blocks is clever and the proof appears correct.

The negative results for α-Rényi/KL divergences (Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3) and the coverage profile (Proposition 4.5) are simple two-point constructions that crisply isolate the 'rare-event' pathology, and the section clearly explains why truncation alone (uniform vs. exponential penalization) does not restore evaluability, plus a margin-condition positive result (Theorem 4.8).

The perplexity analysis (Section 5) connects the theory to practice: showing that nll/perplexity cannot weakly evaluate TV or β-restricted KL (Theorem 5.3), that β-restricted KL is not strongly evaluable at all (Theorem 5.4, with a nontrivial averaging-over-ground-truths argument), and recovering a positive result under a Δ-closeness assumption (Proposition 5.6) using a Hellinger-distance argument. This gives a principled explanation for known empirical complaints about perplexity.
Writing is generally clear, the problem setup is precise, and open questions (estimability vs. strong evaluability, real-valued IPM dichotomy, β-restricted KL) are honestly stated.
weaknesses: The impossibility part of Theorem 3.2 (no c' < 3 weak evaluability for every infinite-VC binary class) is under-argued. The proof merely asserts that a c'-evaluator for d_F 'implies we can properly perform density estimation with multiplicative factor c' < 3, which conflicts with Theorem 19 in Bousquet et al. (2019), in which d_F = TV.' An infinite-VC class does not in general contain (or simulate) all binary functions, so the reduction from a lower bound for the specific class defining TV to an arbitrary infinite-VC class is not established in the text. This is a central optimality claim and needs a complete, correct reduction or a direct construction.

A substantial portion of the negative results formalizes phenomena that are largely known or folklore: unbounded likelihood ratios make cross-entropy/perplexity estimates unreliable, and TV is not estimable from samples without support assumptions (the paper itself credits Bousquet et al., 2019 for the TV case). The novelty lies mainly in packaging these within the new framework rather than in the individual impossibility results.

The framework evaluates a pair of known, explicitly specified models q1, q2 using samples only from q⋆, in the worst case over all distributions. Many practical evaluation regimes (where the models' pathologies are constrained by training, or where metrics are computed with model samples as well) fall outside this model, so the practical force of, e.g., the perplexity impossibility results (which rely on adversarially tiny probabilities on adversarial points) is qualitative rather than prescriptive.

The positive result for the coverage profile (Theorem 4.8) requires both a lower-bound assumption on q⋆ and an (N, α) margin assumption on the likelihood ratios; the sample complexity scales with 1/(α²γ) and 1/γ via union bounds. These assumptions essentially remove the discontinuity that causes the impossibility, so the positive result is somewhat expected, and its practical applicability is limited.

Some related literature is missed: there is an established body of work on minimax estimation and impossibility of estimating f-divergences/KL/entropy functionals from samples without tail or smoothness assumptions (e.g., minimax divergence-estimation literature), which is directly relevant to Theorems 4.2/4.3 and should be discussed to properly delineate what is new.

Minor presentation issues: Definition 2.3 places the implication inside the probability statement, which is unusual and deserves a remark on randomized algorithms; Theorem 3.2's second-bullet sample complexity min{O((2+log(1/δ))/ε²), Õ(8 log^{3/2}(1/δ)/ε^{5/2})} is not explained (where the second rate comes from is unclear in the proof); Theorem 3.6's proof interacts subtly with the 'sufficiently small ε, δ (threshold may depend on q1, q2)' clause and should be written out more carefully; the Hellinger footnote constant (c ≾ 1.1233) appears without derivation.

There are no experiments or worked examples instantiating the theory on concrete model classes (e.g., which test classes actually arise in LLM evaluation and what their VC/fat-shattering dimensions are), which would strengthen the claimed relevance to generative-model evaluation.

strengths: The paper poses a clean and well-motivated question: which evaluation metrics for generative models can be reliably computed from finite IID samples, and formalizes this via a two-tier notion of evaluability (strong vs. weak/c-approximate) tied to ranking two candidate models against ground-truth data.

The binary IPM result (Theorem 3.2) is a pleasingly clean dichotomy: finite VC dimension yields strong evaluability, while infinite VC dimension yields exactly 3-weak evaluability with a matching lower bound, correctly connecting the evaluability question to the Yatracos/Bousquet et al. (2019) density-estimation machinery.

The no-finite-taxonomy result (Theorem 3.6) is a genuinely interesting and relatively novel contribution, showing that estimable IPMs do not admit a VC-dimension-like universal parameter governing sample complexity; the diagonalization-style construction is sound.

The analysis of perplexity/nll as a score function (Section 5) is the most practically resonant part: showing nll cannot weakly evaluate TV distance or β-restricted KL in general, but can evaluate TV under a semi-realizable Δ-closeness assumption (Proposition 5.6), with a nice Hellinger-based argument, gives a principled explanation for empirically observed perplexity failures.

The negative results (Rényi, KL, coverage profile) are stated clearly, hold even under a lower-bound assumption on q* mass (Assumption 4.6), and the paper is honest about what is not proven (e.g., optimality of the factor 3 in the real-valued case is left open). Proofs are provided in full in the appendix.
weaknesses: The access model is under-specified and arguably unrealistic for the motivating application. Score functions and algorithms are granted full knowledge of the model distributions q (e.g., s(q, S_eval) = d_F(q, q̂) requires evaluating the IPM between q and the empirical distribution exactly, and the nll score requires evaluating densities q(x) at arbitrary points). For generative models such as LLMs — the stated motivation — one typically has sample access or at best autoregressive density evaluation, and the paper does not discuss how its results transfer under weaker access. This weakens the claimed relevance to generative-model evaluation in practice.

A substantial fraction of the results is a repackaging of prior work. The upper and lower bounds of Theorem 3.2 follow directly from Bousquet et al. (2019) (the proof in Appendix A is essentially a triangle-inequality argument on top of their Theorem 8 and Theorem 19); the bounded-test results (Theorem 3.8 first bullet, Proposition 3.4 first bullet) are standard uniform-convergence corollaries. The genuinely new material is concentrated in a few theorems (3.6, 5.3, 5.4), making the overall contribution feel thinner than the four-bullet contribution list suggests.

The negative results rest on degenerate, adversarial two- or three-point constructions where the discriminating event has vanishingly small probability under q*. While logically valid, these constructions say little about metrics on realistic data distributions, and the paper offers no empirical or semi-parametric evidence that the identified pathologies (rare-event sensitivity, threshold discontinuity of the coverage profile) actually arise for real generative models or real evaluation pipelines. For a paper framed around LLM evaluation, the complete absence of any experiment or case study is a notable weakness.

The framework evaluates only pairwise ranking against a ground truth q* that itself emits IID samples, and the evaluability definition requires correctness only when the algorithm commits to one of two models. Many practical questions (absolute quality estimation, evaluation when q* is unknown or non-IID, benchmark-style multi-task evaluation) fall outside the framework, and the paper does not clearly delineate these scope restrictions up front.

Several claims of breadth are asserted rather than established: the extension of negative results to 'a broader subclass of tail-sensitive f-divergences' is only conjectured, the real-valued IPM dichotomy (Proposition 3.4) is explicitly weaker than the binary case with the factor-3 optimality left open, and the β-restricted KL analysis ends in open questions. The resulting picture is a collection of examples rather than a satisfying general characterization.

Presentation issues: the main text is very short (14 pages including a one-page open-questions section) and leans heavily on the reader consulting the appendix even for intuition about the main theorems; the related-work positioning against Devroye-type distribution-testing and property-estimation literature (which studies closely related estimability questions) is thin, and there is no discussion of limitations or ethics, which for a paper making broad claims about evaluation methodology would have been appropriate.

strengths: The paper poses a clean and well-motivated question — when can a performance metric for generative models be reliably evaluated from finite held-out samples — and formalizes it via a two-tier notion of evaluability (strong vs. c-weak) that is easy to state and use, with a helpful summary table (Table 1).

Theorem 3.2 provides a sharp dichotomy for binary-valued IPMs (strong evaluability iff finite VC dimension; otherwise 3-weak evaluability, with a matching impossibility for any c < 3), and the paper honestly positions this as an extension of Bousquet et al. (2019).

Theorem 3.6 (no finite taxonomy of sample complexities for estimable IPMs) is a genuinely new and interesting structural result, showing that unlike supervised learning, no VC-like single parameter governs the sample complexity of estimable IPMs; the diagonalization construction is clean.

The negative results are well-executed: the α-Rényi/KL impossibility (Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3), the coverage profile impossibility even under a mass lower-bound assumption (Proposition 4.5) together with a margin-conditioned positive result (Theorem 4.8), and the β-restricted KL results (Theorems 5.3, 5.4) give a coherent story that tail-sensitivity and threshold discontinuity are the fundamental obstructions. The proof of Theorem 5.4 in particular is nontrivial and carefully done.

The perplexity analysis (Section 5) yields practically interpretable takeaways: nll/perplexity is worst-case sensitive and geometrically misaligned with robust metrics, but can evaluate TV distance under a ratio-closeness (semi-realizable) assumption (Proposition 5.6), with a Hellinger-based argument.
The open questions section (Section 6) is candid and useful, and the paper is generally clearly written with complete proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The headline dichotomy (Theorem 3.2) is largely a repackaging of Bousquet et al. (2019): the upper bound is a black-box application of their Theorem 8 and the lower bound is by contradiction with their Theorem 19 for TV. It is not fully clear that their density-estimation guarantee applies verbatim to arbitrary binary test classes with unbounded VC dimension (their setting is TV/Yatracos-style); the authors should state precisely which structural properties of F are needed. This makes the paper's most prominent 'nearly complete characterization' partially derivative.

Several other results are close to expected or follow from short standard arguments: the bounded-test results (Hoeffding), Theorem 3.8's second bullet (a three-point construction), and the Rényi/KL impossibility, whose proof is a standard rare-event construction. The conceptual novelty is real but the technical depth is uneven across sections.

The connection to generative models in practice is loose: the framework treats evaluation as comparing full joint distributions over documents, whereas LLM perplexity evaluates conditional next-token distributions under teacher forcing; the paper does not discuss how (or whether) the impossibility results transfer to the autoregressive/conditional setting that actually motivates the work.

The impossibility results rely on worst-case adversarial constructions (arbitrarily small probabilities on specific points, unbounded likelihood ratios) that practitioners may consider degenerate; the paper would benefit from a discussion of natural distributional assumptions (e.g., bounded density ratios, as in Assumption 5.5) under which the negative results weaken, to calibrate their practical significance.

Gaps and rough edges in statements: the 3-weak upper bound for real-valued IPMs (Proposition 3.4) is not shown to be tight (acknowledged as open, but this undercuts the 'nearly complete characterization' claim); the sample complexity in Theorem 3.2 contains apparent typos ('O(2 + log(1/δ)/ε²)'); Definition 2.3's guarantee is stated only for pairwise output-conditional implications, and the relationship between this comparison-based definition and single-model scoring deserves more care (only partially addressed via Definition 2.4).

Some minor presentation issues: duplicate footnote numbering (footnote 3/4 repeated), inconsistent notation (q̂ vs. q̂ usage in the proof of Theorem 3.2 where the triangle-inequality chain is not fully rigorous as written, e.g., the first inequality d_F(q⋆,q1) ≤ d_F(q̂,q1) + d_F(q̂,q⋆) needs q̂'s guarantee stated relative to both candidates), and no discussion of limitations beyond the open-questions section.

No empirical component; while acceptable for a theory paper, even small illustrative experiments (e.g., instability of perplexity-based ranking under the constructed distributions) would strengthen the bridge between theory and practice.
